We won 𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹 in UIUC's URSA Research Program! This past semester, I worked on improving a computer vision model for solving the VQL (Visual Query Localization) problem with region encoder networks, alongside Akash Danda and mentored by Savya Khosla . Our goal was to extend the existing model (called RELOCATE) to support custom user queries and run the entire pipeline efficiently on any device. We achieved around a 60% success rate, significantly outperforming other existing localizers. Throughout this project, I learned how to grow from failure in research, balance model accuracy with deployment constraints, and translate theoretical ideas into practical systems that actually run outside the lab. Link to the repo: https://lnkd.in/ghwutqbj Huge thanks to Stuti Bhatia and the entire URSA team for such a rewarding experience, and to my teammate and mentor for their guidance and collaboration throughout the semester.

Last week I wrapped up my time as a Cloud Platforms and Telematics Intern at Ford Motor Company in Detroit, MI. I’m grateful for the opportunity I had to contribute to Ford Pro Telematics, a software suite used around the world to connect business owners, managers, and drivers to their fleet of vehicles. Over the course of my internship, I was able to work on new features, improve existing functionality, and take on projects that challenged me to grow as a software engineer. From presenting my work before executives to collaborating with Design and QA, I gained important technical and communication skills that will undoubtedly benefit me for years to come. More importantly, I had the opportunity to work alongside a great group of engineers as well as meet many new friends from across the country. Thank you to Brandy Joe Plambeck , Carly Langer , and Sky Holland for having me aboard, and I look forward to carrying what I’ve learned this summer into my future endeavors.

LinkedIn Shitpost #1: This semester has brought me down to my knees. Unrealistic expectations and ambitions I had for myself, shaped by the success of friends crippled my confidence and created unbounded fear of follopwing through. Often, I halted short of getting started. I would overthink and overprepare, scared of the uncertainty of what it would reveal to me on the otherside. And when I do follow through, every flaw I tried to bury is now staring back alive. Cope. Recover. Avoid. Inspiration. Eager start. Stumble. Fall. Repeat. I saw the man I thought disintegrate before my eyes. Following through has now become harder than ever. Last year, I was diagnosed with Plantar Fasciitis from running. I was impatient, eager to get back to what I loved. I should have foregone the nonessential and allowed it to rest, but because I felt a sense of urgency in every event and opportunity, I crossed what should have been my boundary. It was very revealing of my character, which I am not proud of. It’s paradoxical when I say that I need to keep my momentary ambition tendencies in check. It is about learning to prioritize your values and knowing when it is fine to be distracted. There’s a motto that I really like: “Start now, figure out later when problems inevitably arise”. So I will be taking a gap year. I have no idea who I am nor what I stand for or what I should stand for. I had put on myself the expectation that I will become a certain person by the end of it. Instead, I now humbly say that I have no idea where I am going. That’s the point. I will strive. I will hit dead ends. I will end up where I started. Heck, sometimes the 8 year old me will show through. But I remind myself life is not linear.

We're coming out of stealth. We've built our first racks after a successful A0 tapeout, $1B+ in customer contracts, and $800m raised. Early customer tests show us achieving SOTA throughput, latency, and power efficiency on inference workloads. Our first racks ship this summer. We're a team of 400+ engineers from NVIDIA, Google TPUs, Broadcom, SK Hynix, TSMC, & more. We're backed by Jane Street, HRT, Two Sigma, and Jump, with strategic investment from VentureTech Alliance. We're excited to deepen our partnership with the world's leading semiconductor manufacturer. Our Series B was led by Stripes, with participation from Ribbit Capital, Radical Ventures, Positive Sum, Primary, & Argo. Our inference systems are built to push the entire pareto curve on frontier models, including many-trillion parameter MoEs, long context, and agentic workloads. Today, we're sharing two breakthroughs to make this happen: Low-Voltage Inference (LVI) for high throughput workloads. Today, AI chips can't scale FLOPs without thermal throttling. As FLOPs utilization increases, AI chips draw more power and downregulate clock speed. This often results in sustained inference throughput under half of peak FLOPs. Chips in other industries solve the power problem by running at lower voltages. Bitcoin miners run at under 3x the voltage of AI chips! We’ve designed a new architecture to run our chip’s math blocks at under half the voltage of most AI chips. This enables multiple times the FLOPs density of AI chips today. Cluster-Scale Memory (CSM) for low latency workloads. Today's AI chips using HBM can’t achieve SRAM-level decode speeds due to memory subsystem and interconnect bottlenecks. SRAM-only chips have lower FLOPs density and memory capacity, sacrificing throughput. You’re forced to make a tradeoff: serve at much slower speeds, or run at low batch sizes and suffer from higher costs. When running large MoE models, token routing across experts requires sending data through a deep memory hierarchy and a networking switch to reach a destination expert. Each memory layer inherently adds latency; thus, the best layer is no layer. We’ve designed a new architecture that creates a shared low-latency memory pool across the entire scale-up domain. We use a proprietary ultra-low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnect to enable dramatically faster memory access across chips. Our HBM/SRAM hybrid design solves both memory capacity and mem2mem latency, enabling high throughput and interactivity simultaneously. CSM improves latency and avoids today's cost, reliability, yield, thermal, and compute tradeoffs of SRAM-only chips, 3D DRAM chips, or optics. We're scaling production as fast as possible. We built a 2MW datacenter in our office and opened a Taiwan factory for 24/7 engineering. Performance, roadmap, and more updates are coming this summer. If this excites you, join us to build the future of gigawatt-scale inference: https://lnkd.in/gaQBX-Fz .

Happy to announce that our work AC3S: Adaptive Conditioning for 3D-Aware Synthetic Data Generation has been accepted to #ECCV2026 ! We introduce a diffusion-based framework for 3D-aware synthetic data generation. This framework employs an adaptive visual prompt modulator and a multi-agent VLM system for generating textual prompts. Together, these components ensure both scalability and high-quality datasets for various 2D and 3D vision tasks. Project page (Coming soon) Thank you Yaoyao Liu for your guidance and help from my collaborators Qiran Hu , Wufei Ma , and Sarthak Jain .

The founder pipeline nobody talks about: squash courts. For all its intensity, squash is still one of the most underrated racquet sports in the world. It does not have tennis' prestige, badminton's scale, padel's momentum, or pickleball's U.S. growth story. But once you start looking at the founders and operators who came through squash courts, the pattern is hard to ignore: Founder of WHOOP — Harvard squash Co-founder of Affirm , now GP at a16z — Harvard squash Co-founder of Cursor — MIT squash Founders of Pure — Columbia squash Founder of Takt — Princeton squash Founder of Taya — Stanford squash Co-founder of Fulcrum — Columbia squash Founder of Relay.app — Stanford squash Co-founder of Sparta — Cal squash Founder of Kinect AI — Cal squash I do not think that is random. Squash gives you nowhere to hide. You are trapped in a box with your opponent, physically exhausted, making decisions in real time against someone taking your space, your rhythm, and your confidence. No coaching calls. No team to absorb the mistake. No one to swap in. You are fully liable. That does something to a person. It trains you to think fast, adapt mid-rally, digest hard losses, and earn every win. And it forces you to compete with a high degree of sportsmanship — because in squash, your character is visible on every single point. Squash produces a specific type of operator: competitive, analytical, self-directed, and comfortable being deeply uncomfortable. Most of the reps happen when no one is watching, back corner of a club, just you iterating. A startup is just a bigger box. How does your sport shape how you build, lead, or decide?
